claims.source: Adult-onset, EC-specific knock-down of eIF4e by RNAi alone increased expression of H3 and H4 to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 and H4 p<0.01; post-hoc test, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Adult-onset, knock-down of Atg5 ubiquitously by RNAi had no effect on increased histone expression in response to rapamycin treatment in intestines of flies at 20 days of age.
claims.source: Adult-onset, knock-down of Atg5 ubiquitously by RNAi had no effect on increased histone expression in response to rapamycin treatment in intestines of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 and H4 p>0.05; post-hoc test, NS p>0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Adult-onset bortezomib treatment (2 µM) had no effect on increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
claims.source: Adult-onset bortezomib treatment (2 µM) had no effect on increased expression of H3 and H4 in response to rapamycin treatment in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 4 biological replicates of 10 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA, interaction, H3 and H4 p>0.05; post-hoc test, NS p>0.05, ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment did not disturb histone incorporation into chromatin.
claims.source: We observed that histone H3 remained in chromatin in intestines of both control and rapamycin-treated flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that rapamycin did not disturb histone incorporation into chromatin.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The number of mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomes in the intestine of rapamycin-treated flies was substantially higher than in controls after a short (1 min) MNase digest.
claims.source: The number of mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomes in the intestine of rapamycin-treated flies was substantially higher than in controls after a short (1 min) MNase digest.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MNase digestion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Over-expression of histones H3 and H4 in ECs elevated the number of nucleosomes in intestines as much as did rapamycin treatment, with no further increase in the combined treatment.
claims.source: Over-expression of histones H3 and H4 in ECs elevated the number of nucleosomes in intestines as much as did rapamycin treatment, with no further increase in the combined treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MNase digestion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment induced a substantial chromatin rearrangement in ECs, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in both young (10-day-old) and middle-aged (40-day-old) flies.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment induced a substantial chromatin rearrangement in ECs, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in both young (10-day-old) and middle-aged (40-day-old) flies (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Knock-down of either histone H3 or H4 in adult ECs by RNAi blocked the rapamycin-induced chromatin rearrangement.
claims.source: Knock-down of either histone H3 or H4 in adult ECs by RNAi blocked the rapamycin-induced chromatin rearrangement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: EC-specific over-expression of H3 and H4 recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment on chromatin arrangement, with no further effect in the presence of rapamycin.
claims.source: EC-specific over-expression of H3 and H4 recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment, with no further effect in the presence of rapamycin (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Rapamycin did not affect the amount of HP1, but it altered its distribution, by expanding it across the nucleus in ECs.
claims.source: Rapamycin did not affect the amount of HP1, but it altered its distribution, by expanding it across the nucleus in ECs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of HP1 distribution.

claims.claim: Blocking-increased expression of H3 or H4 in response to rapamycin treatment did not affect the amount of HP1 but abolished HP1 expansion to the whole nucleus in response to rapamycin treatment.
claims.source: Blocking-increased expression of H3 or H4 in response to rapamycin treatment did not affect the amount of HP1 but abolished HP1 expansion to the whole nucleus in response to rapamycin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claims.claim: Over-expression of H3 and H4 in ECs recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment on HP1 distribution, with no additional effect in the presence of rapamycin.
claims.source: Furthermore, over-expression of H3 and H4 in ECs recapitulated the effect of rapamycin treatment on this phenotype, with no additional effect in the presence of rapamycin (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Adult-onset knock-down of H3 or H4 by the 5966GS driver alone had no effect on lifespan of control flies, but completely blocked the lifespan extension by rapamycin.
claims.source: Adult-onset knock-down of H3 or H4 by the 5966GS driver alone had no effect on lifespan of control flies, but completely blocked the lifespan extension by rapamycin (Figure 4A, B; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data and log-rank test statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A, B and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment reduced pH3-positive cell number in the intestine.
claims.source: In line with the previous study (Fan et al., 2015), rapamycin treatment reduced pH3-positive cell number, a proxy for ISC proliferation (Biteau et al., 2010), in the intestine (Figure 4D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 4D-F, and is consistent with a previous study (Fan et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Knock-down of H3 or H4 in adult ECs substantially attenuated the effect of rapamycin on ISC proliferation.
claims.source: Knock-down of H3 or H4 in adult ECs substantially attenuated the effect of rapamycin on ISC proliferation (Figure 4D, E) and on intestinal dysplasia in old flies (50-day-old) (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 4D, E, G.

claims.claim: Adult-onset expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs extended lifespan (log-rank test, p=0.001) and had no additional effect on lifespan in the presence of rapamycin (Rapamycin vs. Rapamycin + RU, p=0.48).
claims.source: Adult-onset expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs extended lifespan (log-rank test, p=0.001) and had no additional effect on lifespan in the presence of rapamycin (Rapamycin vs. Rapamycin + RU, p=0.48).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data and log-rank test statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced ISC proliferation in intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
claims.source: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced ISC proliferation in intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 23–24 intestines, two-way ANOVA, interaction, p<0.001; post-hoc test, ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced intestinal dysplasia in 50-day-old flies.
claims.source: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs reduced intestinal dysplasia in 50-day-old flies (n = 9–12 intestines, two-way ANOVA, interaction, p<0.01; post-hoc test, ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia quantification and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Rapamycin had a substantial impact on the entire transcriptome in the intestine, which increased with age.
claims.source: Rapamycin had a substantial impact on the entire transcriptome in the intestine, which increased with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), with modest changes in gene expression at day 10, and substantial changes at days 30 and 50 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: Expression of autophagy-related genes (e.g., Bchs, Diabetes and obesity regulated (DOR), Stat92E, Atg4a, and Atg8a) were affected by rapamycin treatment.
claims.source: Although we did not detect any significant enrichment of specific biological processes by Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, we noticed that expression of autophagy-related genes (e.g., Bchs, Diabetes and obesity regulated (DOR), Stat92E, Atg4a, and Atg8a) were affected by rapamycin treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on expression of the Bchs and DOR transcripts but not the Stat92E transcript.
claims.source: Quantitative RT-PCR on RNA isolated from fly intestines showed that EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on expression of the Bchs and DOR transcripts but not the Stat92E transcript (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Over-expression of H3 and H4 altered the expression of Bchs and DOR transcripts similarly to rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination.
claims.source: Conversely, over-expression of H3 and H4 altered the expression of Bchs and DOR transcripts similarly to rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination (Figure 5A), suggesting that increased histone expression mediated increased expression of transcripts of autophagy-related genes Bchs and DOR in response to rapamycin.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs mediated enrichment of H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and HP1 on Bchs and DOR transcriptional start sites in the intestine of flies at 20 days of age.
claims.source: Expression of H3/H4 in adult ECs mediated enrichment of H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and HP1 on Bchs and DOR transcriptional start sites in the intestine of flies at 20 days of age (n = 3 biological replicates of 25 intestines per replicate, two-way ANOVA;post-hoc test, compared to controls, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 did not affect phospho-S6K levels, in either the presence or the absence of rapamycin.
claims.source: As expected, rapamycin greatly decreased phospho-S6K levels, but EC-specific expression of H3/H4 did not affect phospho-S6K levels, in either the presence or the absence of rapamycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment resulted in hyperphosphorylation of Atg1, shown by a slower-migrating band on western blot.
claims.source: Furthermore, rapamycin treatment resulted in hyperphosphorylation of Atg1, shown by a slower-migrating band on western blot (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), in line with previous studies (Memisoglu et al., 2019; Yeh et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and is consistent with previous studies (Memisoglu et al., 2019; Yeh et al., 2010).

claims.claim: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 alone did not cause hyperphosphorylation of Atg1.
claims.source: However, EC-specific expression of H3/H4 alone did not cause this effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 decreased the amount of Atg8a-II and Ref(2)P to the same degree as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination.
claims.source: EC-specific expression of H3/H4 decreased the amount of Atg8a-II and Ref(2)P to the same degree as did rapamycin treatment, with no additional effect of their combination (Figure 5C), suggesting that increased histone expression mimicked the effect of rapamycin treatment on autophagy activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta in intestines.
claims.source: In line with a previous study (Bjedov et al., 2010), rapamycin treatment increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta in intestines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) while EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and is consistent with a previous study (Bjedov et al., 2010).

claims.claim: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the increase in LysoTracker-stained puncta in response to rapamycin.
claims.source: In line with a previous study (Bjedov et al., 2010), rapamycin treatment increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta in intestines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) while EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Expression of H3/H4 increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, and neither treatment affected the number of Cyto-ID-stained puncta.
claims.source: Reciprocally, expression of H3/H4 increased the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta to the same extent as did rapamycin treatment, and neither treatment affected the number of Cyto-ID-stained puncta (Figure 5D), suggesting that expression of H3/H4 in ECs did not disturb autophagic flux.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment attenuated the age-related loss of the bicellular junctional protein coracle.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment attenuated the age-related loss of the bicellular junctional protein coracle (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and is consistent with previous studies (Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).

claims.claim: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on maintenance of coracle levels at EC junctions.
claims.source: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on maintenance of coracle levels at EC junctions, while expression of H3/H4 resulted in maintenance of coracle similarly to rapamycin treatment, without further effect of their combination (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Expression of H3/H4 resulted in maintenance of coracle similarly to rapamycin treatment, without further effect of their combination.
claims.source: EC-specific knock-down of H3 by RNAi abolished the effect of rapamycin on maintenance of coracle levels at EC junctions, while expression of H3/H4 resulted in maintenance of coracle similarly to rapamycin treatment, without further effect of their combination (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment resulted in a reduction of barrier function loss, and this effect was abolished by knock-down of H3 in adult ECs.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment resulted in a reduction of barrier function loss, and this effect was abolished by knock-down of H3 in adult ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Smurf assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Expression of H3/H4 in ECs resulted in a modest, but significant, reduction in the number of Smurf flies and had no further effect in the presence of rapamycin.
claims.source: Expression of H3/H4 in ECs resulted in a modest, but significant, reduction in the number of Smurf flies and had no further effect in the presence of rapamycin (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Smurf assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Reduction of Atg5 substantially reduced the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta following increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs.
claims.source: Reduction of Atg5 substantially reduced the number of LysoTracker-stained puncta following increased expression of H3/H4 in ECs (Figure 6A), suggesting that Atg5 was required for the effect of increased histone expression on autophagy activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 alone did not affect lifespan, but it abolished the increase in response to increased expression of H3/H4.
claims.source: EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 alone did not affect lifespan, but it abolished the increase in response to increased expression of H3/H4 (Figure 6B; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 completely blocked the effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on intestinal dysplasia and maintenance of gut integrity.
claims.source: Furthermore, EC-specific knock-down of Atg5 completely blocked the effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on intestinal dysplasia and maintenance of gut integrity (Figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia and Smurf assay data shown in Figure 6C, D.

claims.claim: Knock-down of Atg1 inhibited the increase in autophagy in response to over-expression of H3/H4.
claims.source: Knock-down of Atg1 inhibited the increase in autophagy in response to over-expression of H3/H4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and blocked the beneficial effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on gut health (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Knock-down of Atg1 blocked the beneficial effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on gut health.
claims.source: Knock-down of Atg1 inhibited the increase in autophagy in response to over-expression of H3/H4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and blocked the beneficial effects of increased expression of H3/H4 on gut health (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Reduction of Bchs expression by RNAi in combination with either rapamycin treatment or over-expression of H3/H4 in ECs blocked the increase of LysoTracker-stained puncta in response to H3/H4.
claims.source: Reduction of Bchs expression by RNAi in combination with either rapamycin treatment or over-expression of H3/H4 in ECs blocked the increase of LysoTracker-stained puncta (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) in response to H3/H4, suggesting that Bchs was crucial for the effects of increased histone expression on autophagy activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Knock-down of Bchs alone had no effect on lifespan, but it abolished the effects of both rapamycin treatment and histone over-expression on lifespan.
claims.source: Knock-down of Bchs alone had no effect on lifespan, but it abolished the effects of both rapamycin treatment and histone over-expression on lifespan (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary files 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, and Supplementary files 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Knock-down of Bchs abolished the effects of rapamycin treatment and histone over-expression on intestinal dysplasia and gut integrity.
claims.source: It also abolished the effects of these treatments on intestinal dysplasia and gut integrity (Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intestinal dysplasia and Smurf assay data shown in Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: EC-specific over-expression of Bchs was sufficient to recapitulate the effects of rapamycin and histone over-expression on autophagy, lifespan, and intestinal homoeostasis.
claims.source: Conversely, EC-specific over-expression of Bchs was sufficient to recapitulate the effects of these treatments on autophagy, lifespan, and intestinal homoeostasis (Figure 7E–H; Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence, lifespan, intestinal dysplasia, and Smurf assay data shown in Figure 7E-H and Supplementary file 7.

claims.claim: Neither knocking down nor over-expressing Bchs in ECs influenced mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of Atg1.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that neither knocking down nor over-expressing Bchs in ECs influenced mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of Atg1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: Expression of all of the core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) in the small intestine of female mice was significantly increased by rapamycin treatment at 12 months and 22 months of age.
claims.source: Expression of all of the core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) in the small intestine of female mice was significantly increased by rapamycin treatment at 12 months and 22 months of age (Figure 8A, B), consistent with our results from flies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A, B.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment induced a modest, but significant, chromatin rearrangement in epithelial cells in villi, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in cells of rapamycin-fed mice at 12 months and 22 months of age.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment induced a modest, but significant, chromatin rearrangement in epithelial cells in villi, with marked accumulation of chromatin at the nuclear envelope in cells of rapamycin-fed mice at 12 months and 22 months of age (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment increased nucleosome occupancy in 22-month-old rapamycin-fed mouse intestines.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment also increased nucleosome occupancy in 22-month-old rapamycin-fed mouse intestines (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MNase digestion assay data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Expression of Wdfy3 transcript in the small intestine in 22-month-old mice increased in response to rapamycin treatment.
claims.source: Furthermore, expression of Wdfy3 transcript in the small intestine in 22-month-old mice increased in response to rapamycin treatment (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast.
claims.source: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast (Feser et al., 2010), the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans (Ni et al., 2012), and human senescent cells (Ivanov et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Feser et al., 2010; Ni et al., 2012; Ivanov et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans.
claims.source: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast (Feser et al., 2010), the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans (Ni et al., 2012), and human senescent cells (Ivanov et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ni et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in human senescent cells.
claims.source: Histone H3 protein levels decrease in aged yeast (Feser et al., 2010), the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans (Ni et al., 2012), and human senescent cells (Ivanov et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ivanov et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Over-expression of core histones H3 and H4 extended replicative lifespan in yeast.
claims.source: Concordantly, over-expression of core histones H3 and H4 extended replicative lifespan in yeast, potentially attenuating the age-related loss of nucleosomes, transcriptional dysfunction, and genomic instability in aged yeast cells (Feser et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Feser et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Lowered activity of the IIS/mTOR network by nutritional, genetic, or pharmacological interventions can extend lifespan and reduce age-related pathologies in multiple organisms.
claims.source: Lowered activity of the IIS/mTOR network by nutritional, genetic, or pharmacological interventions can extend lifespan and reduce age-related pathologies in multiple organisms (Fontana et al., 2010; Kenyon, 2010; Niccoli and Partridge, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Fontana et al., 2010; Kenyon, 2010; Niccoli and Partridge, 2012).

claims.claim: Reduction of mTORC1 activity by genetic manipulation of key components of mTORC1, TOR or Raptor, extends lifespan in yeast, nematode worms C. elegans, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, and mice.
claims.source: Reduction of mTORC1 activity by genetic manipulation of key components of mTORC1, TOR or Raptor, extends lifespan in yeast, nematode worms C. elegans, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, and mice (Johnson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Johnson et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment extends lifespan in diverse organisms, including mice, and attenuates a broad spectrum of age-related functional decline and diseases.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment extends lifespan in diverse organisms, including mice, and attenuates a broad spectrum of age-related functional decline and diseases (Johnson et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Johnson et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Lifespan extension by rapamycin in Drosophila requires reduced S6K activity and increased autophagy downstream of mTORC1.
claims.source: Lifespan extension by rapamycin in Drosophila requires reduced S6K activity and increased autophagy downstream of mTORC1 (Bjedov et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bjedov et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Genetic manipulations that reduce S6K activity extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
claims.source: Consistently, genetic manipulations that reduce S6K activity (Kapahi et al., 2004; Selman et al., 2009) or activate autophagy (Pyo et al., 2013; Ulgherait et al., 2014) extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kapahi et al., 2004; Selman et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Genetic manipulations that activate autophagy extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
claims.source: Consistently, genetic manipulations that reduce S6K activity (Kapahi et al., 2004; Selman et al., 2009) or activate autophagy (Pyo et al., 2013; Ulgherait et al., 2014) extend lifespan in both Drosophila and mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Pyo et al., 2013; Ulgherait et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Activating expression of autophagy-related genes can prevent age-related dysfunction in a variety of tissues.
claims.source: More generally, activating expression of autophagy-related genes can prevent age-related dysfunction in a variety of tissues; for instance, limiting intestinal barrier dysfunction, memory impairment, and muscular dystrophy in animal models (Hansen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hansen et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The Drosophila intestine consists of four major cell types: intestinal stem cells (ISCs), multipotent enteroblasts, secretory enteroendocrine cells, and polyploid ECs.
claims.source: The fly intestine contains four major cell types: intestinal stem cells (ISCs), which are mitotically active throughout the life course, multipotent enteroblasts, secretory enteroendocrine cells, and polyploid ECs that are the major differentiated cell type (Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013) and established knowledge about Drosophila intestinal anatomy.

claims.claim: Histones can undergo increased translation via a non-canonical, eIF3-mediated mechanism.
claims.source: However, previous studies have demonstrated notable exceptions to this translational suppression, including histones, which can undergo increased translation via a non-canonical, eIF3-mediated mechanism (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Thoreen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Thoreen et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Inhibition of eIF4 components can enforce mRNA translation through an eIF3-specialised pathway.
claims.source: This result was in line with the previous study showing that inhibition of eIF4 components can enforce mRNA translation through an eIF3-specialised pathway (Lee et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2016).

claims.claim: ECs play a key role in modulating ageing and age-related pathologies.
claims.source: ECs play a key role in modulating ageing and age-related pathologies (Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Age-related intestinal pathologies are driven by both unregulated ISC division and loss of homeostasis in ECs.
claims.source: Age-related intestinal pathologies are driven by both unregulated ISC division (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008) and loss of homeostasis in ECs (Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018), both of which reduce lifespan.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008; Bolukbasi et al., 2017; Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017; Salazar et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Rapamycin reduces age-associated ISC proliferation, attenuating intestinal dysplasia.

results.result: Rapamycin treatment extends lifespan in Drosophila and specifically increases histone H3 and H4 protein expression in the intestine but not in brain, muscle, or fat tissues. The intestine has much lower basal histone expression than other tissues, and rapamycin increases histone expression by 2 days after treatment initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide converging evidence from lifespan assays (C1), western blots (C2-C6), and statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA) showing tissue-specific effects of rapamycin on histone expression. The data demonstrate appropriate sample sizes (n=4 biological replicates), statistical rigor, and consistent findings across multiple time points and tissues.

results.result: Rapamycin's effect on histone protein levels is post-transcriptional in young flies but attenuates age-related increases in histone transcripts in older flies. In young flies (1-5 days), rapamycin does not affect H3/H4 transcript levels, but in older flies (30-50 days), it reduces the age-associated increase in histone transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by qRT-PCR data with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) and biological replicates (n=3-4). The findings demonstrate age-dependent effects and support the conclusion that rapamycin acts post-transcriptionally in young flies but has transcriptional effects in aged flies.

results.result: Dietary restriction (DR) does not influence histone H3 and H4 expression in the intestine, distinguishing the rapamycin effect from general caloric restriction.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 is supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA showing no effect of DR (1× vs. 2× SYA food) on histone expression. This control experiment strengthens the specificity of the rapamycin effect, though only one DR condition was tested.

results.result: Rapamycin treatment does not alter intestinal cell type composition or enterocyte polyploidy, indicating that increased histone expression is not due to changes in cellular architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification and two-way ANOVA with adequate sample sizes (n=5-6 intestines). These control experiments rule out alternative explanations for increased histone protein levels, though C10 notes a reduction in ISC mitosis.

results.result: Rapamycin increases histone expression through eIF3-mediated translation rather than through canonical eIF4-dependent translation. Cycloheximide blocks the rapamycin-induced histone increase, and knockdown of eIF3d or eIF3g abolishes it, while eIF4e knockdown mimics rapamycin's effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15 provide mechanistic evidence through pharmacological (cycloheximide) and genetic (RNAi) approaches with appropriate controls and statistics (two-way ANOVA, n=4 replicates). The findings are internally consistent and align with prior literature on non-canonical translation mechanisms for histones.

results.result: Autophagy (Atg5 knockdown) and proteasome inhibition (bortezomib) do not affect rapamycin-induced histone expression, indicating that protein turnover does not mediate this effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are supported by western blot data and two-way ANOVA showing no interaction effects. These negative controls help establish that rapamycin acts through translation rather than protein degradation pathways.

results.result: Rapamycin treatment increases nucleosome occupancy in the intestine without disturbing histone incorporation into chromatin. Overexpression of H3/H4 in enterocytes recapitulates this effect with no additional increase from rapamycin.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 are supported by subcellular fractionation and MNase digestion assays. The data demonstrate that increased histones lead to increased nucleosomes, though quantification details for the MNase assay are limited in the text.

results.result: Rapamycin induces chromatin rearrangement with accumulation at the nuclear envelope in enterocytes, an effect that requires increased histone expression. H3/H4 overexpression alone is sufficient to recapitulate this chromatin reorganization.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification with appropriate statistical analysis (linear mixed model). The genetic epistasis experiments (knockdown and overexpression) provide strong evidence for histone-mediated chromatin reorganization.

results.result: Rapamycin alters HP1 distribution by expanding it across the nucleus without changing total HP1 levels. This redistribution requires increased histone expression and can be recapitulated by H3/H4 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing HP1 redistribution. The genetic experiments demonstrate that histone expression mediates this effect, providing evidence for heterochromatin reorganization.

results.result: Increased histone expression in enterocytes is required for rapamycin-induced lifespan extension and reduction of ISC proliferation. Knockdown of H3 or H4 in adult enterocytes completely blocks rapamycin's effects on lifespan and partially blocks effects on ISC proliferation and intestinal dysplasia.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by lifespan assays with log-rank tests and ISC proliferation quantification with two-way ANOVA. The genetic requirement experiments provide strong evidence that histones mediate rapamycin's longevity effects, though the partial effect on dysplasia (C29) suggests additional mechanisms may contribute.

results.result: Overexpression of H3/H4 in adult enterocytes is sufficient to extend lifespan, reduce ISC proliferation, and decrease intestinal dysplasia, with no additional benefit from rapamycin treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are supported by lifespan data (log-rank test), ISC proliferation quantification, and dysplasia measurements with appropriate statistics (two-way ANOVA). The lack of additive effects with rapamycin suggests histones act in the same pathway.

results.result: Rapamycin has a substantial, age-dependent impact on the intestinal transcriptome, with modest changes at day 10 and substantial changes at days 30 and 50. Autophagy-related genes including Bchs, DOR, Stat92E, Atg4a, and Atg8a are affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by RNA-seq data with adequate sequencing depth (≥37.5 million reads per sample, n=3 replicates). The PCA and differential expression analyses are appropriate, though the lack of significant GO enrichment (mentioned in C34) suggests the transcriptional changes may be modest or dispersed.

results.result: Increased histone expression mediates transcriptional regulation of autophagy genes Bchs and DOR (but not Stat92E) through altered enrichment of histone modifications (H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me3) and HP1 at their transcriptional start sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by qRT-PCR and ChIP-qPCR data with appropriate sample sizes (n=3-4 replicates) and statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA). The mechanistic link between histone levels and epigenetic regulation of specific autophagy genes is well-established through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: H3/H4 overexpression does not affect mTORC1 activity (phospho-S6K levels) or Atg1 hyperphosphorylation, indicating that histones act downstream of mTORC1 and independently of the canonical mTORC1-Atg1 autophagy initiation pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by western blot data showing differential effects of rapamycin versus H3/H4 overexpression on S6K and Atg1 phosphorylation. These negative results are important controls that help establish the mechanism of action, though sample sizes are not explicitly stated for all experiments.

results.result: H3/H4 overexpression activates autophagy as measured by decreased Atg8a-II and Ref(2)P levels and increased LysoTracker-stained puncta, without affecting Cyto-ID staining. This effect requires H3 expression and mimics rapamycin treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by western blots and immunofluorescence with appropriate quantification and statistics (linear mixed model, n≥6 intestines). The use of both LysoTracker and Cyto-ID provides evidence that autophagic flux is not impaired, strengthening the conclusion of autophagy activation.

results.result: Increased histone expression improves intestinal barrier function by maintaining the junctional protein coracle and reducing the proportion of Smurf flies. H3 knockdown abolishes rapamycin's effects, while H3/H4 overexpression recapitulates them.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification of coracle and Smurf assays with appropriate statistics (linear mixed model, two-way ANOVA, n=9-12 intestines or 10 replicates of 15-20 flies). The genetic epistasis experiments provide strong evidence for histone-mediated barrier function maintenance.

results.result: Autophagy genes Atg5 and Atg1 are required for the beneficial effects of H3/H4 overexpression on autophagy activation, lifespan extension, and intestinal health. Knockdown of either gene abolishes these effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by immunofluorescence, lifespan assays, and intestinal health measurements with appropriate controls and statistics. The genetic requirement experiments establish that canonical autophagy machinery is necessary downstream of histones, though the specific roles of Atg1 and Atg5 differ (C53-C54 vs C50-C52).

results.result: The selective autophagy cargo adaptor Bchs is both necessary and sufficient for histone-mediated effects on autophagy, lifespan, and intestinal health. Bchs knockdown abolishes these effects, while Bchs overexpression recapitulates them.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by comprehensive genetic experiments including immunofluorescence, lifespan assays, and intestinal health measurements with appropriate statistics. The necessity and sufficiency experiments provide strong evidence that Bchs is a key mediator of the histone-autophagy axis.

results.result: Bchs manipulation does not affect mTORC1-mediated Atg1 phosphorylation, indicating that Bchs acts independently of the canonical mTORC1-Atg1 autophagy initiation pathway.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by western blot data showing no effect of Bchs knockdown or overexpression on Atg1 phosphorylation. This negative result is important for establishing the mechanism of action, though sample sizes are not explicitly stated.

results.result: In mice, rapamycin treatment increases expression of all core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) in the small intestine, induces chromatin rearrangement in intestinal epithelial cells, increases nucleosome occupancy, and increases Wdfy3 (mammalian Bchs homolog) transcript expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by western blots, immunofluorescence, MNase assays, and qRT-PCR in mice at 12 and 22 months of age with appropriate statistics (two-way ANOVA, linear mixed model, n=3 per group). The conservation of effects across species strengthens the translational relevance, though sample sizes are modest.

results.result: The study establishes an mTORC1-histone-autophagy axis where rapamycin increases histone expression via eIF3-mediated translation in enterocytes, leading to chromatin reorganization, transcriptional activation of autophagy genes (particularly Bchs), and improved intestinal health and longevity. This axis is at least partially conserved in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 represent the integrated conclusions of the study, supported by the collective evidence from multiple experimental approaches in both flies and mice. The mechanistic pathway is well-established through genetic, pharmacological, and molecular experiments, though C98's claim about therapeutic potential is somewhat speculative.
